query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys under tribo-corrosion, the interplay of mechanical wear and corrosion is governed by the repeated formation, disruption, and reformation of a protective passive oxide film. Mechanical action breaks down the film, locally exposing the reactive alloy surface to the corrosive environment, while subsequent oxidation partially restores the film. This cycle ultimately controls the overall degradation rate.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (e.g., a CrMoNbWV-based HEA) with an initially intact, protective passive oxide layer formed under static conditions.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA sample to simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., controlled sliding or oscillatory contact) in a corrosive electrolyte to induce tribo-corrosion.
generation.conditions: Perform the experiment in a controlled laboratory tribo-corrosion cell where mechanical wear and corrosive attack occur concurrently, while maintaining constant temperature, pH, and flow conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The passive oxide film integrity and its cyclic disruption/regeneration at the wear track.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear disrupts the passive oxide film, exposing fresh metal that is more susceptible to corrosion. Corrosion rapidly reforms a passive layer, which is then again mechanically removed. This repeated cycle of film breakdown and repair controls both the wear rate and the corrosion kinetics, collectively governing the total degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline sample exposed only to the corrosive environment, the tribo-corrosion sample will show increased overall degradation with higher localized corrosion rates and enhanced wear damage. The degradation pattern should exhibit periodic surface changes corresponding to film rupture and reformation cycles.
generation.baseline: An identical HEA sample maintained in the same corrosive environment without mechanical wear.
generation.boundary: The prediction should hold for HEAs where surface passivation by oxide formation is the dominant corrosion protection mechanism. It may fail or be obscured in alloys that do not form protective films or where bulk deformation processes dominate the wear response.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the enhancement in corrosion and wear rates is uncertain due to variability in oxide film formation kinetics, mechanical stress distribution during wear, and specific alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens with identical composition. Expose one set to a controlled tribo-corrosion test (simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive electrolyte) and the other set to a static corrosion test (only the corrosive electrolyte). Monitor the surface film dynamics in real time using techniques such as in situ XPS or Raman spectroscopy, and measure wear track profiles and corrosion currents using profilometry and potentiodynamic polarization.
measurements: Surface oxide film thickness (via XPS or Raman spectroscopy)
Wear track depth and morphology (via profilometry/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passive oxide film does not exhibit cyclic disruption and regeneration under tribo-corrosion conditions, or if the corrosion and wear rates in the tribo-corrosion sample are statistically indistinguishable from the static corrosion baseline, then the hypothesis that the cyclic behavior of the passive film governs the coupled degradation process is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm
